## Kiriakou on the Bustamante résumé (2026)

On The Pocket in July 2026, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) disputed the public presentation of [Andrew Bustamante](/wiki/andrew-bustamante)'s [CIA](/wiki/cia) career. On his account, Bustamante was never an operations officer: *"he was a special operations officer or staff operations officer — that's an assistant to the operations officers. So this notion that he was running out there running around the world grabbing bad guys, kicking asses, and taking names is just simply not true."* Kiriakou also rejects Bustamante's public claim that money is *"the only objective measure of success"* and that people with less than a million dollars are ignored — *"see, but this is coming from a guy who never recruited a source in his entire career"* — and dismisses Bustamante's stated plan to move his children to a developing country to *"appreciate America"* as *"who wouldn't want to get malaria when you're six years old?"*<Cite t="22:19" /><Cite t="22:49" /><Cite t="23:19" /><Cite t="23:51" /><Cite t="27:29" /><Cite t="28:01" />

three-felonies-a-day.body_append:
## Kiriakou's on-record use of the book (2026)

On The Pocket in July 2026, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said Harvey Silverglate's *[Three Felonies a Day](/wiki/three-felonies-a-day)* is the framework he reaches for whenever he is asked whether he could have avoided his own [Espionage Act](/wiki/espionage-act) prosecution. Silverglate's argument, as Kiriakou paraphrases it, is that the American criminal code is so over-broad — with so many overlapping and vaguely drafted federal statutes — that *"the average American on the average day, going about his or her normal business, commits three felonies every single day."* The takeaway Kiriakou uses on the point is blunt: *"if they want to get you, they're going to get you."*<Cite t="01:01" /><Cite t="01:32" />

john-kiriakou.body_append:
## Compartmentalising the CIA — and why the divorce hurt more than prison

On The Pocket in July 2026, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said the reason his 2018 divorce carries the [PTSD](/wiki/john-kiriakou) his imprisonment does not is that he had deliberately spent his CIA career refusing to let the agency become his whole life. *"So many people make the CIA their entire existence — everything in life is the CIA. They have two, three, four, five, six even marriages. Just because family's never the focus, it's always the job."* He recalled a boss whose mother died while he was overseas and who had spent every prior rest-and-relaxation window returning to Langley to read into cases rather than fly back to see her — *"now my mother's dead. I have nobody"* — and vowed not to become that person. *"I always had home I could go to. And then I didn't have home. And that's what kind of did me in."*<Cite t="13:58" /><Cite t="14:28" /><Cite t="14:59" /><Cite t="15:31" /><Cite t="16:03" />

## CIA affinity groups

Kiriakou describes the [CIA](/wiki/cia)'s use of on-campus affinity groups — a softball league, a flag football league, an LGBTQ group, a choir, a quilting club, a cooking club, discounted baseball and football tickets at the employee activity centre — as an intentional device to keep employees inside the security perimeter: *"anything you wanted to do in life, you could do it right there at the CIA."* The design premise, on Kiriakou's account, is that *"everybody's cleared, and so you can talk about work while you're quilting or playing baseball or whatever."* Kiriakou says he played softball but treated the rest as *"just not right."*<Cite t="16:34" /><Cite t="17:05" />

## Federal prison as career criminality

At the [Bureau of Prisons](/wiki/john-kiriakou), Kiriakou said, guards routinely commit felony theft as a career practice — including, on one witnessed occasion, backing an F-150 pickup up to the commissary loading dock to steal an entire pallet of Pop-Tarts (and similar pallets of batteries, A&D ointment and StarKist tuna) for resale on Facebook Marketplace and eBay.<Cite t="07:12" /><Cite t="07:45" /><Cite t="08:15" /> In one particularly acute episode, Kiriakou said, two special-investigative-service officers called him in to tell him a Kurdish prisoner had been ordered from a number in Pakistan to kill him — while telling the Kurdish prisoner Kiriakou had been ordered from a number in Washington to kill him — in an evident attempt to get them to kill each other. Kiriakou reported the episode to the *Huffington Post* and treats it as one of the felonies of the guards themselves: *"I'm the bad guy for reporting it."*<Cite t="08:15" /><Cite t="08:46" />

## The Greek terrorism files

On switching from analysis to operations, Kiriakou said, he was assigned to review thousands of pages of files on Greek terrorism dating back to the 1960s. He said the material was so shocking that when he audibly muttered *"oh my god"* while turning a page, an unknown voice on the other side of the office partition answered *"you going through the Greek files? That's what everybody says when they go through the Greek files."* Kiriakou notes the documents remain *"currently improperly classified"* and he cannot describe their contents.<Cite t="29:33" /><Cite t="30:04" /><Cite t="30:37" />
